title: Judgment (CCC 1021–1022)
hookLine: at death each person is judged by love

lines: A COURTROOM, A BOOK, A GAVEL.
cards: A courtroom. A huge book. Every lie you ever told, read out loud.
A stern face, a gavel. Maybe a scale, good deeds on one side and bad ones on the other, and you watching to see which way it tips. That's what the word judgment can drag in.
Now hold it next to a sentence from a Spanish friar you met earlier on this path, John of the Cross: at the evening of life, he said, we will be judged on love. Not on the scale. On love.

teach.h: ONCE TO DIE, AND AFTER, JUDGMENT.
teach.b: Hebrews says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "it is appointed unto men once to die, and after this the judgment." The Catechism teaches that each person receives this judgment at the very moment of death.
It's called the particular judgment, because it's about one particular life. And it's immediate.
At death, the Catechism says, each soul receives its eternal destiny at once: heaven, either through a purification or directly, or else separation from God forever.
Catholics point to the thief crucified next to Jesus, who asked only to be remembered, and heard: "this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Not someday. Today.
The Catechism quotes John of the Cross's line about being judged on love at the evening of life.
It fits Jesus's own story of the sheep and the goats, where the question isn't how much you knew but whether you fed the hungry.

teach.h: ONE LIFE, THEN ALL OF THEM.
teach.b: Catholics say that at death a person sees their life in Christ's light, and the question is how they loved, and whether they accepted or refused his love.

The Church also speaks of a final judgment at the end of time, when Christ returns and the whole of history is brought into the light. The particular judgment is one life. The last judgment is all of them together.
And the one who judges, Catholics say, is the same one who died for the person being judged: justice, yes, but from a judge who wants each person home.

how: Catholics profess in the Creed that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, and many make a nightly examination of conscience, looking back over the day with the question of how they loved.

o: a life seen in Christ's light and weighed by love
a sentence given to everyone only at the end of time
a scale weighing your good deeds against the bad

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: one life, at the moment of death
all of history, at the end of time

s: the Catechism says judgment waits until the end of time for everyone
it teaches a particular judgment at the moment of death, and a final judgment at the end.
the Catechism quotes John of the Cross on being judged on love
at the evening of life, we will be judged on love.
in Catholic teaching, the judge is the one who died for the person judged
Christ judges, the same Christ Catholics say gave his life for each person.

games.q: you're the thief crucified beside Jesus. you have no time to fix anything. you ask him only to remember you. what does he say?
o: this day thou shalt be with me in paradise.
come back when you've made up for it.
games.why: this day, in paradise. Catholics see in it both the immediacy of judgment and the mercy of the judge.

practice: Choose one person close to you, a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, a coworker, and look at the last month with them, honestly but kindly.
Where did you love well, and where did love run thin, a short word, a missed call, a silence?
Name both without beating yourself up, then ask what more love would look like here this week; if you pray, you can ask for help to do it.

wordCard.voice: Judgment. In Catholic teaching, the moment at death when each life is seen in Christ's light, and judged on love, followed by a final judgment at the end of time. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: judgment, decision. the root of the English word crisis.

carryVoice: Your line: judged by love. On love, not on a scale. Day three hundred twenty-five, done.
